projects.title: Fast Credit *Mobile App.*
projects.hook: Leading Fast Credit’s first mobile app, bringing manual loans and investments into a digital customer journey.
projects.summary: I led product design for Fast Credit’s first mobile app. The business wanted to reach more people, automate manual loan and investment processes and grow into a fintech. Working with another designer, product, engineering and QA, I helped turn that ambition into an implemented app and continued refining it through employee testing, staff feedback and observation.

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Me, 1 product designer, 1 PM, 5 engineers, 2 QA, 2 Devops

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: UX · UI · Design system · Implementation review · Iteration

glance.problem: Fast Credit’s core loan and investment processes were manual. Its first mobile app needed to support wider reach, automation and the company’s move into fintech.
glance.solution: I led design and worked with the PM to replace immediate Tier 3 onboarding with basic registration and in-app tier upgrades, while the team moved some processing into the background.
glance.impact: The implemented app enabled digital acquisition and brought new customers. The Data Analytics Team reported 41K+ total registered accounts as of November 2026, across different KYC and activation stages; a design-attributable growth rate is not established.

blocks.heading: A new acquisition channel. *41K+ registered accounts.*
blocks.body: The implemented app brought new customers to Fast Credit through a digital channel. Its Data Analytics Team reported 41K+ total registered accounts as of November 2026.
blocks.label: Contribution and measurement
blocks.text: Design contributed to making this digital channel usable and accessible as part of the wider product and implementation effort. The account total includes different KYC and activation stages, rather than only fully onboarded or active customers. A quantitative growth lift attributable to design alone has not been established.

blocks.heading: Everyday finance. *One connected product.*
blocks.caption: AI-assisted presentation of the supplied login and investment designs. Original interface screens appear below.

blocks.heading: Fast Credit’s first app. *A new way to serve customers.*
blocks.body:
Fast Credit’s core loan and investment processes were manual. The company wanted to reach a wider customer base, automate these processes and grow into a fintech. This was its first mobile app.

I led product design with another designer, working with the PM, engineering and QA. The work connected the business’s ambition to the customer’s journey: register, understand the offering, verify an account and use financial services through a mobile channel.

blocks.heading: Get people into the app. *Let verification progress inside it.*
blocks.body: The original onboarding journey took everyone straight to Tier 3. It also depended on immediate backend and network responses, creating long waits that blocked progress. I aligned with the PM on a different sequence: basic initial registration, followed by Tier 1, Tier 2 and Tier 3 upgrades inside the app.
blocks.label: Change the sequence and the processing
blocks.text: The team moved some processing into the background so the customer did not have to wait at every step. The design contribution was to separate initial access from later account upgrades, make the progression understandable and reduce how much of the journey depended on an immediate response.

blocks.heading: Map the journey, *including the interruptions.*
blocks.body: The supplied wireframes show onboarding, OTP and dashboard-entry flows. The design considered states such as an existing number, unaccepted terms, network delays and BVN validation in progress.
blocks.caption: Onboarding, OTP and dashboard-entry flows

blocks.heading: A shared language for *a connected product.*
blocks.body: Fellix typography, Fast Credit’s brand green and consistent components established a common visual language. The mobile layouts use a 390 × 844 baseline, with defined spacing and states to support implementation.

specs.label: System
specs.value: Shared components, colours and interaction states

blocks.heading: Everyday finance, *connected through one interface.*
blocks.body: The designs span investments, loans and account management. They bring balances, next actions and account-upgrade paths into a consistent interface.

blocks.heading: 250+ employees tested *the implemented app.*
blocks.body:
More than 250 company employees participated in internal testing across teams. They used the implemented app for salary receipts, transfers, bill payments and account upgrades.

Issues were reported through a dedicated email address and recorded in a shared sheet tracker. This was a company-wide testing effort after implementation; the count refers to employee testers, not interviews or research sessions I personally conducted.

blocks.heading: Keep feedback connected *to the work.*
blocks.body: The internal testing process gave design, product, engineering and QA a shared route for identifying and following up issues.

items.title: Use the implemented app
items.body: Employees tried real financial tasks, including salaries, transfers, bills and upgrades.

items.title: Report an issue
items.body: Feedback was sent to the dedicated testing email address.

items.title: Track the issue
items.body: Reports were recorded in a shared sheet tracker for team follow-up.

items.title: Review and iterate
items.body: Design questions and implementation issues were considered with the relevant colleagues.

blocks.heading: Staff complaints led to alternatives. *Their feedback shaped the revision.*
blocks.body:
Before exploring these alternatives, I heard complaints from internal staff and observed how they used the app. I then tested revised interface directions with staff. Their qualitative feedback favoured the revisions as more appealing, smoother and more effective.

This was qualitative internal A/B feedback; a preference percentage was not recorded.
blocks.caption: Internal A/B interface comparison: dashboard, transaction history, transfer and loan

items.label: Dashboard
items.body: The alternatives compare minimal icon-led actions with a green balance area, visible funding actions and recent transactions.

items.label: Transaction history
items.body: The exploration adds search, filters and calendar controls to a date-grouped transaction list.

items.label: Transfers
items.body: The designs compare separate action buttons with a transfer interface that includes beneficiaries, source account, limit information and a remark field.

items.label: Loans
items.body: The later direction gives repayment context more space: outstanding balance, tenor, progress and monthly repayment, alongside the next available action.

blocks.heading: Use the verified record *to reduce repeated entry.*
blocks.body:
A further design iteration addressed the mismatch risk created when someone manually enters a name alongside a BVN record. The revised journey starts with the BVN, verifies ownership and asks the person to confirm the returned details.

This describes the rationale and flow from my account of the project. A verified reduction in failed upgrades is not available.

items.title: Enter BVN
items.body: Provide the BVN used for the account verification.

items.title: Verify ownership
items.body: Enter the code sent to the phone number linked to the record.

items.title: Confirm details
items.body: Review the returned information rather than entering the name again.

items.title: Complete liveness check
items.body: Follow the identity-check step in the upgrade flow.

items.title: Secure the account
items.body: Set the required PIN and password.

blocks.heading: The linked phone number *still matters.*
blocks.body: The BVN-first journey depends on access to the phone number associated with the record. If that number is unavailable, receiving a code remains a barrier. This is an unresolved design consideration; no verified failure rate or completed alternative is claimed here.

blocks.heading: What I carry *into the next project.*

items.label: Connect the business and the journey
items.body: The first app created a digital route to services that had been manual. Design helped make that route usable as part of a shared delivery effort.

items.label: Listen while the product is used
items.body: Staff complaints, observation and comparative feedback gave me concrete directions to explore. Company-wide employee testing also surfaced issues in the implemented product.

items.label: Know what a number describes
items.body: Registered accounts show the scale of the new channel. They do not, on their own, establish activation, completion or the amount of growth caused by a particular design decision.

projects.title: Chopbaze *Website.*
projects.hook: Design leadership and hands-on AI-assisted development for a food marketplace.
projects.summary: I lead the design, delegate selected sections and review the work. All AI-assisted website development is mine.

glance.problem: Give Chopbaze’s bulk-food marketplace a public website that communicates the idea to prospective buyers and vendors.
glance.solution: I lead the design, delegate selected sections and review the work. All AI-assisted website development is mine.
glance.impact: A live public website introducing the food offer and connecting customers and vendors to the product.

blocks.heading: Lead the design. *Build the website.*
blocks.body: I lead the design, delegate selected sections and review the work. All AI-assisted website development is mine.

blocks.heading: Start with the occasion, *then explain the offer.*
blocks.caption: Live homepage captured 12 November 2026.

blocks.heading: Make the next step *easy to understand.*
blocks.body: The site presents food categories and portion sizes, a four-step ordering explanation, and customer controls such as preparation preferences and scheduling. A vendor section explains the partner proposition. Gathering examples connect the service to real occasions.

blocks.heading: Design for *shared occasions.*
blocks.caption: The gatherings section of the live website.

blocks.heading: AI-assisted code. *My responsibility.*
blocks.body: I used AI to develop the entire website. I own the implementation work, while selected design sections were delegated to a designer working under my direction. The presentation mockup above uses captures of the live site; the original captures are shown here.

blocks.heading: *Reflection*
blocks.body:
Working on Chopbaze reinforced that designing a website goes beyond making a product visually appealing. The bigger challenge was translating a growing business idea into a clear, understandable experience for people encountering the brand for the first time.

As both a co-founder and design lead, I had to think beyond individual screens, balancing business objectives, user expectations, content clarity, and visual consistency. Delegating parts of the design also taught me that leadership isn't about designing everything yourself, but about providing direction and ensuring every contribution supports a shared vision.

Building the website with AI-assisted development expanded my understanding of the relationship between design and implementation. AI accelerated execution, but making decisions about the experience, reviewing the output, and taking responsibility for quality remained my job.

**My biggest takeaway:** Good design is not measured by how much you create, but by how effectively you communicate what matters. The next step is validating that clarity with real customers and vendors, rather than assuming that a polished, launched website automatically communicates the right message.

projects.title: Fast Credit *Website.*
projects.hook: A self-initiated redesign that clarified the product offering and brought a loan calculator into the journey.
projects.summary: I initiated an audit after concerns from marketing and sales about the website. The redesign consolidated the information architecture, clarified product content and added a loan calculator to help visitors understand repayment before applying.

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Audit · IA · UX · UI · Stakeholder case

glance.problem: A website that confused visitors and under-delivered for marketing and sales, with no one assigned to fix it.
glance.solution: A self-initiated audit, a consolidated information architecture, and a custom loan calculator that answers the visitor's real question: can I afford this?
glance.impact: The redesigned website shipped with consolidated product information and a loan calculator. Verified engagement, bounce-rate and lead-quality measurements are not available.

blocks.heading: Turn a shared concern *into a design proposal.*
blocks.body:
Marketing and sales raised concerns about how the website explained Fast Credit’s services. I reviewed the site independently, organised the issues into an audit and presented a redesign proposal to leadership.

This account is reconstructed from my involvement in the project. The existing website images and redesign artifacts show the structural and visual changes.

blocks.heading: An audit of *structure and clarity.*
blocks.caption: Before: five sparse product pages, no hierarchy, weak calls to action

items.label: 01 · Dated
items.body: The existing visual treatment did not clearly surface the institutional information available to support trust.

items.label: 02 · Navigation
items.body: **A maze of five product pages** (Loans, Investments, Fast Thrift, Public Workers, BNPL) to understand one offering.

items.label: 03 · Overload
items.body: **Every page explained everything.** No hierarchy, no obvious next step anywhere in the journey.

items.label: 04 · Sparse
items.body: **Content spread thin.** Pages that needed depth were empty; pages that belonged together were siloed.

items.label: 05 · Imagery
items.body: Generic photography had little connection to the product story or the customers the site was intended to serve.

items.label: 06 · Layout
items.body: **No consistent grid.** Arbitrary spacing and broken rhythm made the site feel assembled in parts.

blocks.heading: Five sparse pages became *one purposeful structure.*
blocks.body: The first decision was structural, not visual: consolidate navigation so every product earned its place in the hierarchy. Then I added something no stakeholder had asked for but every visitor needed: **a loan calculator**, answering the only question that matters before applying: *can I afford this?*
blocks.caption: Desktop and mobile wireframes: restructured IA and the new loan calculator

blocks.heading: A homepage that finally *tells the story.*
blocks.body: The redesigned homepage brings the value proposition, product offering and institutional information into a clearer hierarchy. App-download links, benefits, testimonials and partner content support the route into the product.
blocks.caption: Shipped homepage: hero, products, benefits, testimonials, partners

blocks.heading: Every page rebuilt, including *the one nobody asked for.*
blocks.body: About, every loan product, the calculator, blog, and contact with office locations, designed at desktop and mobile breakpoints.
blocks.caption: About, Loans, Fast Pearl, Calculator, Blog, Contact

blocks.heading: A clearer website. *An implemented calculator.*
blocks.body:
The website redesign shipped, including the loan calculator and a revised product structure. These are observable delivery outcomes.

Earlier performance figures were stakeholder estimates and have not been independently verified. I do not present them as measured engagement improvements or attribute lead quality to the redesign.

items.label: Make the problem visible
items.body: An organised audit gave the team something concrete to review and discuss.

items.label: Support the decision
items.body: The calculator gives visitors repayment information alongside the route to an application.

items.label: Structure shapes the interface
items.body: Consolidating the information architecture guided what the pages needed to explain.

projects.title: Evamor *Store.*
projects.hook: A responsive commerce redesign centred on finding the product and placing an order.
projects.summary: Evamor supplies dispenser water to homes, offices, hotels and restaurants across Lagos. I redesigned the website around product discovery and ordering, with revised navigation, responsive layouts and a clearer order form.

glance.problem: Visitors couldn't find how to order, the mobile experience broke, and the order form asked too much, too early.
glance.solution: A sitemap rebuilt around purchase intent, a persistent Order Now path one click from anywhere, and a one-page order form with transparent pricing.
glance.impact: A shipped, responsive website with a clearer route to ordering. Conversion and sales changes have not been independently verified.

blocks.heading: Make ordering *part of the product experience.*
blocks.body: Evamor serves homes, offices, hotels and restaurants across Lagos. The redesign focused on making its products easier to find and its ordering process easier to understand across desktop and mobile.

items.label: 01 · Navigation
items.body: The ordering route needed more prominence within the site’s structure.

items.label: 02 · Mobile
items.body: The redesign addressed mobile layouts, touch targets and type consistency.

items.label: 03 · Order form
items.body: The form needed clearer information about price and delivery alongside the required customer details.

blocks.heading: Keep the ordering route *easy to find.*
blocks.body: I rebuilt the sitemap around the visitor's real intent (understand the product, trust the brand, place an order) and made Order Now persistent on every page.
blocks.caption: Wireframes: Home, About, Products and Order · desktop and mobile

blocks.heading: Deep ocean blues. *Trust, by association.*
blocks.body: A palette of ocean blues to signal purity, quality and trust. Poppins for clean neutrality that stays legible on small, bright screens.

blocks.heading: Home, story, products, order: *one cohesive flow.*
blocks.body: About (mission, vision, values), detailed product pages with specs and benefits, and an order page rebuilt for clarity: name, address, phone, a quantity selector and transparent pricing, all on one screen.
blocks.caption: Home, About, Core values, Products and Order

blocks.heading: A complete ordering journey. *An honest outcome.*
blocks.body:
The redesigned site shipped with responsive layouts, product information and an order form. Those deliverables are documented in the project images.

Earlier conversion and sales-growth figures were stakeholder estimates without independently verified measurement. They are not presented here as established results or proof of causation.

items.label: Start with the customer’s task
items.body: A visible ordering path helped organise both navigation and page content.

items.label: Design across screen sizes
items.body: Product information, form fields and calls to action need the same care on a phone as on a desktop.

projects.title: Cedaa *Yoghurt.*
projects.hook: Twenty years of craft, hidden behind a template. Three weeks to make the website as good as the yoghurt.
projects.summary: A Nigerian dairy with 20+ years of heritage, NAFDAC and SON certification, and a loyal customer base, all represented by a generic template with no mobile design. In three weeks I delivered a refined identity, a 12-column design system, and a mobile-responsive site that finally reflects the brand.

glance.problem: A premium product line undermined by a template site: no identity, no brand story, no mobile experience.
glance.solution: Evolution, not revolution: keep the brand's equity, refine it into a deliberate system, and give every product room to sell itself.
glance.impact: A mobile-ready brand platform in three weeks, with a system the team can extend without breaking it.

blocks.heading: Every ingredient of a premium brand. *A template undermining all of it.*
blocks.body: Cedaa had 20+ years of operation, NAFDAC and SON certifications, a loyal customer base across Ogun State, and a product line that deserved shelf space next to national players. The website was the one thing working against them.
blocks.caption: Before: a generic template: flat identity, no emotional pull, no mobile layout

items.label: 01 · Identity
items.body: **No brand presence.** A generic pink hero and slider; nothing signalled quality, heritage or a 20-year story.

items.label: 02 · Mobile
items.body: **No mobile design.** FMCG buyers research on their phones, especially for home delivery. Desktop-only meant invisible.

items.label: 03 · Products
items.body: **Good photography, buried** in a flat grid with no hierarchy, no variants and no reason to choose.

items.label: 04 · Story
items.body: **Factual but cold.** Mission, vision and values were listed, never felt.

blocks.heading: Evolution, not revolution. *Elevate the brand, don't replace it.*
blocks.body: The brief was elevation, not a rebrand. I kept the existing red and white and refined them into a deliberate palette, with a warm off-white base that lets product photography breathe. Urbanist brings confident geometry, premium without feeling cold.

blocks.heading: A site Cedaa's team can *scale on their own.*
blocks.body: A benefit-led hero (*Deliciously nutritious. Made for every moment.*), a catalogue tabbed by flavour (Vanilla, Unsweetened, Strawberry, Pineapple), Our Story, Why Cedaa, Core Values, a store finder with maps, newsletter and a full footer. Responsive throughout.
blocks.caption: Hero, Products, Story, Why Cedaa, Values, Find a store, Contact

blocks.heading: From template to *premium brand platform*, in three weeks.

items.label: Brand elevation
items.body: A premium identity that communicates quality, heritage and trust, without starting from scratch.

items.label: Scalable system
items.body: 12-column grid, documented components and tokens. New pages and campaigns ship without breaking the design.

items.label: Mobile-first
items.body: Full mobile alongside desktop, so customers can discover, explore and locate Cedaa on any device.

items.label: Product storytelling
items.body: Each flavour gets its own space: sizes, taste notes, nutrition callouts and photography that makes it desirable.

items.label: Elevation is restraint
items.body: Keep the equity people already recognise; remove the noise around it.

items.label: Systems outlive launches
items.body: Three weeks of work only compounds if the team can extend it without me.

projects.title: Altirev *Election Monitoring.*
projects.hook: Real-time election monitoring for civic organisations across Nigeria.
projects.summary: A multi-role election-monitoring platform for civic organisations, currently in beta. The work focuses on organising information across roles in a time-sensitive setting.

blocks.heading: Election day leaves *no room for error.*
blocks.body: WRITE: who the client is, what civic organisations needed to monitor, and why existing tools failed on election day.

blocks.heading: Every role sees a *different election.*
blocks.body: WRITE: the roles (for example field observers, coordinators, analysts), what each one needs in the moment, and the conditions they work in (network, devices, pressure).

blocks.heading: One platform, *many permissions.*
blocks.body: WRITE: how you structured roles, permissions and navigation so each user only sees what they need.
blocks.caption: Role map / sitemap

blocks.heading: The decision that *made it work.*
blocks.body: WRITE: the hardest trade-off (for example speed of reporting vs. accuracy) and how you resolved it with the team.
blocks.label: Design principle

blocks.heading: Built for accuracy *under pressure.*
blocks.body: WRITE: the key flows you designed: submitting a report, verifying it, watching results live.

blocks.heading: Where it *stands now.*
blocks.body: WRITE: beta status, who is testing it, and the first signals you have (feedback, usage, numbers).

process.title:
Good design continues
*after the handoff.*
process.intro: The common thread across these projects is collaboration: making decisions visible, bringing the right people in, and reviewing the work as it becomes real.

steps.label: 01 · Understand
steps.title: Get clear on *the problem.*
steps.body: Review the brief, existing experience, business needs and available feedback. Be explicit about what is known and what still needs investigation.

steps.label: 02 · Explore
steps.title: Make the journey *tangible.*
steps.body: Map flows and states, compare design directions and build the interface around the task people need to complete.

steps.label: 03 · Align
steps.title: Bring the team *into the decisions.*
steps.body: Work with designers, product and engineering. Assign work where I lead, review it together and coordinate feedback before and during implementation.

steps.label: 04 · Follow through
steps.title: Review the product *as it becomes real.*
steps.body: Support implementation and internal testing. Use reported issues to guide iteration, and distinguish delivery progress from outcomes that still need measurement.

about.pageTitle: I design products that *work in the real world.*
about.pageLead: I work across **hands-on product design, design leadership and implementation collaboration**.
about.body:
I’m Victor Ajibodu, a Product Design and UI/UX Lead in Lagos with 6+ years in product design. I currently lead a team of designers at **Fast Credit Limited**, working on financial experiences across mobile and web.

On the mobile app, I worked with another product designer, product management, engineering and QA. More than 250 company employees tested the implemented app, with issues collected through a dedicated email and shared tracker. That was a team testing effort, not a series of interviews I personally conducted.

I own **the company’s first E-Token product design end to end** and lead the design work for **its first Internet Banking product** by assigning modules, reviewing contributions and coordinating team feedback. E-Token is in TestFlight QA and internal testing; Internet Banking is in development. Their public launch is planned together.

Beyond fintech, my work includes commerce websites and other digital products. The Fast Credit website redesign was self-initiated, and I’m also building Chopbaze as a co-founder.

I care about making the work understandable: what I owned, what the team contributed, what shipped and what still needs evidence.

I work confidently with **Claude and ChatGPT across design, research and coding**. They are part of how I explore ideas, make sense of research, prototype interactions and turn designs into working experiences.
